newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: AIDS pioneer plans South African research centre.
newsitem.headline: AIDS pioneer plans South African research centre.

text.p: French AIDS pioneer Luc Montagnier said on Friday he planned to open a new research centre in South Africa to tackle the epidemic on the continent hardest hit by the deadly disease.
Montagnier, who is credited with isolating the AIDS virus, told a news conference that the centre for southern and eastern Africa would focus on applied research and clinical work.
"We want to learn more about the natural history of AIDS infection in Africa and try to establish new kinds of affordable treatments and also, hopefully, a vaccine," he said.

There had been significant progress recently in developing better AIDS treatments using combinations of virus inhibitors. But the vast majority of patients in developing countries had no access to these costly medicines, he said.

Montagnier said one goal would be to investigate complementary products which might boost the efficacy of expensive drugs produced by the pharmaceutical industry, thereby reducing dosing requirements and cost.
"If we can achieve that, many more people could have access to effective treatment and it would lower the burden on the health system," he said.

Walter Prozesky, president of South Africa's Medical Research Council which will partner Montagnier's World Foundation for AIDS Research and Prevention in the project, said this could include traditional medicines.
University of Stellenbosch researchers, for example, had identified a compound from a traditional medicinal plant which showed considerable promise, he said.
Montagnier, who spent the last week looking at sites for the new research centre, said South Africa was a logical location for his foundation, which already operates in Paris and Abidjan.

South Africa had good laboratory and clinical facilities. Montagnier said President Nelson Mandela had expressed support during talks at the World Economic Forum in Davos earlier this year. Local business has also pledged its backing.
South Africa is also an important epidemiological centre for studying Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS).

Protected in part by the isolation of the apartheid era, the country has lagged the rest of the continent in the spread of the HIV virus which leads to AIDS. But in the last five years it has witnessed Africa's fastest rate of growth in infections.

UNAIDS, the United Nations coordinating agency for the AIDS epidemic, estimates 2.2 million South Africans -- five percent of the population -- are now infected, including an estimated 13 percent of pregnant women.

Elsewhere in southern Africa the story is far worse. More than 18 percent of all adults in Botswana are infected; 17 percent in Zambia and Zimbabwe. In Europe and the United States the epidemic may be on the wane.

"The epidemic is still there and there is still a very fast rate of increase in infections in many countries -- not only Africa, but also southeast Asia, south China, India and South America," Montagnier said.
